Kropyvnytsky Jewish Section

Jewish Cemetery · Kirovohrad Oblast, Ukraine

Not demolished. Kropyvnytskyi has carried five different names across its history — founded as the fortress of Elisaveta in 1754, later Elisavetgrad, then Zinovyevsk (1924), Kirovo (1934), Kirovograd (1939), and finally Kropyvnytskyi after 2016 decommunization — reflecting the shifting political currents of the Russian Empire and USSR. Elisavetgrad was among the first cities where the massive pogrom wave of April 1881 originated, and a further pogrom in 1919 killed between 1,500 and 3,000 people, one of the deadliest single pogroms recorded in this collection; the Jewish community nonetheless grew to nearly 24,000 — almost 39 percent of the city — by 1897, supporting 17 Jewish schools by 1909. German occupation lasted over two and a half years, from August 1941 to January 1944, and most Jews who remained behind perished. A tiny but active Jewish community survives in Kropyvnytskyi today. Its cemetery consists of two Jewish sections: an older one established no later than the 1950s, still receiving occasional burials from descendants of those already interred there, and a newer section opened in the 1990s once the older one filled.
